summary: A 1975 working document specifying a front-end protocol for attaching a Burroughs B6700 computer to an ARPA-style network. The approach is to use a front-end processor with a new protocol, built on earlier concepts from RFC 647.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 705 describes a working protocol between a host and a front-end computer that connects to an ARPANET-like network. The front-end handles network details while the host uses commands to establish paths and exchange data.

questions: what is a front end processor
how does fep abstract network complexity
subtitle: A working host-to-front-end protocol that lets a front-end provide network access.

tldr.problem: A host connecting directly to an ARPANET-like network must implement complex network protocols, which can disrupt its normal operating environment.
tldr.mechanism: The Front-End Protocol lets a host issue commands to an intermediate computer that manages network connections, data paths, replies, and translations.
tldr.outcome: The memo describes a proposed, site-specific protocol for attaching a Burroughs B6700 through a front-end processor. It is explicitly a working document.

facts.label: Commands
facts.value: BEGIN, LISTEN, RESPONSE, MESSAGE, INTERRUPT, END, REPLY

today: RFC 705 is marked as a working document and presents a proposed, site-specific Front-End Protocol for the B6700. Its appendix on host implementations is marked “To be written at a later date.”

sections.title: Delegating Network Protocols
sections.content:
The RFC describes connecting a general-purpose host to an ARPANET-like network through a front-end processor. The host-to-front-end protocol is intended to let the host use network protocols without managing their detailed operation itself.

The document is a working specification for a B6700 attachment and assumes a lower-level line protocol between host and front-end that provides error-free transmission.
sections.plainLanguage: A host can connect to an intermediate computer instead of implementing the network protocols itself. The intermediate computer, called the front-end, handles the network side.

sections.title: Indexes, Paths, and Commands
sections.content:
The host identifies conversations with indexes and the communication paths within them with path numbers. A path can be SEND, RECEIVE, or DUPLEX; a duplex path lets both the host and front-end send MESSAGE commands.

BEGIN establishes outgoing paths, LISTEN waits for incoming connection requests, RESPONSE reports connection results, MESSAGE carries data, INTERRUPT signals an event, END closes paths, and REPLY acknowledges commands and reports success or failure.
sections.plainLanguage: The host opens a conversation and its data paths with commands. Paths can carry data in one direction or both, and replies report whether each command worked.

sections.title: Translation and Flow Control
sections.content:
When BEGIN or LISTEN establishes paths, the host can specify data formats on the host and network sides. The front-end translates MESSAGE data between those formats as needed.

Commands other than REPLY require an acknowledgement. The sender cannot send another command on the same path until it receives a reply; a READY indication also permits another MESSAGE.
sections.plainLanguage: The front-end can translate data between the host's format and the network's format. Replies also control when each side may send more commands or data.

sections.title: Implementation and Scope
sections.content:
The memo includes state diagrams and implementation notes for the front-end and host. Its examples show Telnet, FTP, teleconferencing, and one-way connections using the same indexes and paths.

The protocol leaves the physical line protocol and its implementation dependent on the installation. Appendix D, which was meant to describe host implementations, says it would be written later.
sections.plainLanguage: The protocol is designed to support several kinds of network use, but details of the physical host-to-front-end link depend on the installation. The memo leaves its host-implementation appendix unfinished.
